title: Spinal Nerve and Root
subtitle: Recognizing single-root (segmental) lesions from pain, dermatomal sensory loss, myotomal weakness and reflex changes, and matching them to disc level

points.text: Sensory fibers enter the cord through the dorsal roots; their cell bodies lie in the dorsal root ganglia.
points.quote: enter the spinal cord in the dorsal roots and have their perikarya in the dorsal spinal root ganglia

points.text: Motor fibers come from ventral horn neurons and leave as the ventral roots.
points.quote: arise from the motor neurons located in the ventral horns of the spinal cord and exit the cord as the ventral roots

points.text: After the foramen the nerve splits: the smaller posterior primary rami serve the dorsal trunk skin (and axial muscles).
points.quote: The smaller posterior primary rami supply the skin on the dorsal aspect of the trunk with sensory fibers

points.text: The anterior primary rami supply the limbs, the nonaxial muscles and the lateral and anterior skin of trunk and neck.
points.quote: The anterior primary rami supply the limbs (see Chapter 3), nonaxial skeletal muscles, and skin of the lateral and anterior trunk and neck

points.text: There are 31 pairs of spinal nerves, split by region.
points.quote: There are 31 pairs of spinal nerves—8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, and 1 coccygeal.

coreAnatomy.title: Myotome, dermatome and the cervical map

points.text: A root is identified by its myotome (muscles of one anterior root) and dermatome (skin of one posterior root).
points.quote: each group of muscles supplied by a single anterior spinal root (myotome) and each cutaneous area supplied by a single posterior spinal root (dermatome)

points.text: Segmental sensory and motor signs are what separate a root lesion from a peripheral nerve or plexus lesion.
points.quote: Differentiation from peripheral nerve or plexus lesions thereby depends on the segmental character of the sensory and motor signs and symptoms.

points.text: C5 lesions: sensory disturbance on the lateral arm; biceps and brachioradialis reflexes (C5-C6) may be depressed.
points.quote: The biceps reflex (subserved by segments C5-C6) and the brachioradialis reflex (C5-C6) may be depressed.

points.text: C6 lesions: sensory signs on the lateral forearm, lateral hand and the first and second digits.
points.quote: Sensory signs and symptoms occur on the lateral forearm, lateral hand, and the first and second digits.

points.text: C7 lesions: sensory disturbance on the third and fourth digits; the triceps reflex (C7-C8) may be depressed.
points.quote: Sensory disturbances occur on the third and fourth digits.

points.text: C8 lesions: sensory signs on the medial forearm, hand and fifth digit; the finger flexor reflex (C8-T1) may be depressed.
points.quote: sensory signs and symptoms occur on the medial forearm and hand and on the fifth digit

points.text: L4 lesions: sensory disturbance on the knee and medial leg; the patellar reflex (L2-L4) may be depressed.
points.quote: Sensory disturbances occur on the knee and the medial leg.

points.text: L5 lesions: sensory signs on the lateral leg, dorsomedial foot and large toe.
points.quote: Sensory signs and symptoms occur on the lateral leg, the dorsomedial foot, and the large toe.

points.text: S1 lesions: sensory disturbance on the little toe, lateral foot and most of the sole; the Achilles reflex (S1-S2) is depressed.
points.quote: Sensory disturbances occur on the little toe, lateral foot, and most of the sole of the foot.

points.text: S2-S5 lesions affect the perianal region and may impair bladder and bowel control, with an absent anal wink.
points.quote: Sensory disturbances occur on the calf, posterior thigh, buttock, and perianal region.

localizationRules.rule: Root pain is provoked by raised intraspinal pressure
localizationRules.explanation: Irritation of a dorsal root gives lancinating, electric or burning pain referred to one dermatome or myotome, made worse by coughing, straining, sneezing, Valsalva or spine movement.
localizationRules.quote: characteristically accentuated or precipitated by maneuvers that cause increased intraspinal pressure or stretching of the dorsal nerve root

localizationRules.explanation: Because adjacent dermatomes overlap, one damaged dorsal root may give little or no measurable sensory loss; pain and motor or reflex signs then carry the localization.
localizationRules.quote: Because of the overlap of cutaneous supply by adjacent nerve roots, sectioning of a single dorsal root results in little or no sensory loss.

localizationRules.rule: Root lesions lower the reflex of that segment
localizationRules.explanation: Either a dorsal (afferent) or ventral (efferent) root lesion interrupts the reflex arc, so the stretch reflex subserved by that root is reduced or absent.
localizationRules.quote: with ventral or dorsal lesions, hyporeflexia or areflexia occurs in the muscle subserved by the affected spinal root

localizationRules.rule: Disc level is not root level
localizationRules.explanation: A posterolateral L4-L5 disc hits the L5 root, which exits at L5-S1; a very lateral protrusion can hit L4 and a very medial one can hit S1.
localizationRules.quote: an L4-L5 protrusion that occurs posterolaterally affects the L5 root destined to leave the canal in the L5-S1 foramen

localizationRules.rule: Thoracic roots are localized by sensory findings
localizationRules.explanation: Thoracic and abdominal muscles are hard to test and no stretch reflex is subserved by T2-T12, so sensory symptoms and signs mostly guide the diagnosis.
localizationRules.quote: Therefore, clinical diagnosis relies predominantly on sensory symptoms and signs.

keySyndromes.name: C7 radiculopathy (C6-C7 disc)
keySyndromes.triad: Pain in the dorsal forearm + sensory disturbance on the third and fourth digits + paresis variably in triceps, flexor carpi radialis, extensor digitorum + triceps reflex (C7-C8) may be depressed
keySyndromes.clue: C7 is the commonest cervical radiculopathy; pain may occasionally be subscapular or deep in the breast or chest.
keySyndromes.quote: This nerve root is often compressed by disc herniation at the C6-C7 vertebral level (the most common level of disc herniation)

keySyndromes.name: C6 radiculopathy (C5-C6 disc)
keySyndromes.triad: Pain in the lateral arm and dorsal forearm + sensory signs on the lateral forearm, lateral hand and first and second digits + paresis in biceps, pronator teres, brachioradialis and others + biceps and brachioradialis reflexes may be depressed
keySyndromes.clue: Second most common cervical radiculopathy after C7; thumb and index finger sensory loss (digits 1-2) versus digits 3-4 for C7.
keySyndromes.quote: A monoradiculopathy affecting the C6 nerve root is the second most common level of cervical radiculopathy after lesions of the C7 level

keySyndromes.name: C8 radiculopathy (C7-T1 disc)
keySyndromes.triad: Pain in the medial arm and forearm + sensory signs on the medial forearm, hand and fifth digit + paresis of hand intrinsic and finger flexor muscles + finger flexor reflex (C8-T1) may be depressed + ipsilateral Horner syndrome
keySyndromes.clue: Horner syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis) accompanies C8 and T1 root lesions because sympathetic fibers to the superior cervical ganglia are interrupted.
keySyndromes.quote: Sympathetic fibers destined for the superior cervical ganglia are interrupted, resulting in an ipsilateral Horner syndrome (ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis).

keySyndromes.name: L5 radiculopathy (L4-L5 disc)
keySyndromes.triad: Pain in lower back, buttock, lateral thigh and anterolateral calf + sensory loss on lateral leg, dorsomedial foot and large toe + weakness of ankle and toe dorsiflexion (tibialis anterior, extensor hallucis longus) and gluteus medius + patellar and Achilles reflexes spared
keySyndromes.clue: Reflexes are spared in L5 lesions, whereas the Achilles reflex is depressed in S1.
keySyndromes.quote: L5 root involvement causes lower back, buttock, lateral thigh, and anterolateral calf pain.

keySyndromes.name: S1 radiculopathy (L5-S1 disc)
keySyndromes.triad: Pain in lower back, buttock, lateral thigh and calf + sensory loss on little toe, lateral foot and most of the sole + paresis of gluteus maximus, gastrocnemius, soleus and small foot muscles + Achilles reflex depressed
keySyndromes.clue: The usual posterolateral L5-S1 protrusion gives an S1 syndrome; a very lateral one gives L5.
keySyndromes.quote: Sensory disturbances occur on the little toe, lateral foot, and most of the sole of the foot.

keySyndromes.name: Neurogenic pseudoclaudication of the cauda equina
keySyndromes.triad: Unilateral or bilateral asymmetric buttock, thigh or leg pain after exertion + occasional numbness, loss of reflexes or paresis + relief by rest, waist flexion or sitting
keySyndromes.clue: Most commonly due to lumbar stenosis; must be separated from vascular claudication (Table 4-2), where peripheral pulses are absent and pain is relieved by stopping regardless of position.
keySyndromes.quote: These signs and symptoms are relieved by rest, flexion at the waist, and sitting

boardTraps.text: No sensory loss on examination does not rule out a single-root lesion, because neighboring roots overlap.
boardTraps.quote: the absence of sensory loss does not exclude the possibility of a lesion affecting a single dorsal root

boardTraps.text: Cervical root lesions can be falsely localized one level too high because of intradural communications between neighboring posterior roots.
boardTraps.quote: A lesion may, therefore, be falsely localized clinically to a segment one level higher than its actual location.

boardTraps.text: An inverted radial reflex means spinal cord compression at C5-C6, not just a root lesion: the brachioradialis tap gives no brachioradialis response but brisk finger flexion.
boardTraps.quote: elicits no response by the brachioradialis but a brisk contraction of the finger flexors innervated by the C8-T1 segments

boardTraps.text: The root affected depends on where the disc protrudes, not only on the interspace: a lateral L4-L5 protrusion can involve L4 and a medial one S1.
boardTraps.quote: very lateral L4-L5 protrusion, however, may affect the L4 root traversing the L4-L5 interspace, and a very medial lesion may affect the S1 root

boardTraps.text: The straight leg raise is sensitive but not specific, so a positive test alone does not prove a herniated disc.
boardTraps.quote: reported the accuracy of the straight leg test as 0.80-0.97 sensitive and about 0.4 specific

boardTraps.text: Severe or progressive axillary pain should prompt a search for malignancy in the upper thoracic root region.
boardTraps.quote: Pain in the armpit that is severe or progressive may be indicative of a malignant pathology
